comments.text:
I don't want to directly or individually address the videos discussing the 9070 XT testing I did recently. Those videos did misunderstand the test, but unfortunately I didn’t explain the video as well as I should have, and did suggest that the bulk of the gains in at least one instance were a result of display drivers when really it could have been any number of things. 

To help avoid confusion I should have also labelled the graphs “Review Data” and “Latest Data” rather than review drivers and latest drivers.

The point of the video was to take the review data for the 9070 XT and 5070 Ti, and compare that to what we’re getting now, using the same games and settings featured in the review. This gives us a look at how things have progressed after 4 months, are the margins still the same or has one card improved more than the other?

I wasn’t the first to notice that for whatever reason the 9070 XT had improved in a number of games. @pcgameshardware  first reported a 13% increase in performance for the 9070 XT in Hunt Showdown 1896, 13% in Space Marine 2, 24% for Forza Motorsport, 17% for Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, 23% for Half-Life Ray Traced and 14% for Portal RTX.

Outside of that they tested a range of games I didn’t, meaning many of the 16 games I tested weren’t featured in their content, so I was keen to see what changes might be seen in those titles.

The gains for the 9070 XT and RDNA 4 series in general aren’t just a result of newer drivers, they’re likely a combination of things, such as game updates, platform updates and perhaps even Windows updates. So a simple driver test where you compare the release driver with the latest driver won’t necessarily show the same gains for all games, as all other updates have already taken place.

Just to be clear that wasn’t the purpose of this content, and I think I explained the idea behind the video quite well. As stated in the video the idea was to take the outdated review data for the 9070 XT and 5070 Ti, and compare that to what we’re seeing today. My mistake was focusing on drivers as being the leading cause for the performance gains, which was an assumption on my part.

comments.text:
Yeah neither of them understood the test and unfortunately I didn’t explain the video as well as I should have, and did suggest that the bulk of the gains in at least one instance were a result of display drivers when really it could have been any number of things. To help avoid confusion I should have also labelled the graphs “Review Data” and “Latest Data” rather than review drivers and latest drivers.

The point of the video was to take the review data for the 9070 XT and 5070 Ti, and compare that to what we’re getting now, using the same games and settings featured in the review. This gives us a look at how things have progressed after 4 months, are the margins still the same or has one card improved more than the other?

I wasn’t the first to notice that for whatever reason the 9070 XT had improved in a number of games. @PC Games Hardware first reported a 13% increase in performance for the 9070 XT in Hunt Showdown 1896, 13% in Space Marine 2, 24% for Forza Motorsport, 17% for Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, 23% for Half-Life Ray Traced and 14% for Portal RTX.

Outside of that they tested a range of games I didn’t, meaning many of the 16 games I tested weren’t featured in their content, so I was keen to see what changes might be seen in those titles.

The gains for the 9070 XT and RDNA 4 series in general aren’t just a result of newer drivers, they’re likely a combination of things, such as game updates, platform updates and perhaps even Windows updates. So a simple driver test where you compare the release driver with the latest driver won’t necessarily show the same gains for all games, as all other updates have already taken place.

Just to be clear that wasn’t the purpose of this content, and I think I explained that part of the video idea quite well. As stated in the video the idea was to take the outdated review data for the 9070 XT and 5070 Ti, and compare that to what we’re seeing today. My mistake was focusing on drivers as being the leading cause for the performance gains, which was an assumption on my part.

comments.text:
In your 9070 XT Review video, I wrote this comment:

"6:14 - As a long time Counter-Strike player and a follower of your channel, let me explain something... The game is terribly optimized and should NOT be included in the benchmarks out of the box. The reason being - it has terrible 1% lows on ANY possible configuration because of its engine. CS2 is one of the rare games where capping your FPS via RTSS makes the frametime graph WAY SMOOTHER. Capping it ingame has no effect. From my testing, capping it via nVidia control panel also didn't work as expected, but maybe with the new control panel works now, haven't tested...

Regardless, if you want to properly test CS2 you have to cap the FPS to below the max framerate a GPU can achieve. I'd say 350 should be achievable for most GPUs, which would mean the only difference would be their minimum FPS.

And this leads me to the whole point why I'm writing this comment. The average FPS for the 9070 XT is obviously a driver issue which would eventually get fixed (just like with the 7900 XTX), but what we need to be looking at is the 1% lows, which on the 4k graph is on par with the RTX 4080s (just like in most other games), which are responsible for the smooth gameplay that a game like Counter-Strike MUST HAVE.

I bet (and also wish to see) that if you retest this game with the FPS capped, you'll get a much better graph."

And I was completely right back then!

RDNA 4 is going to be the last of its architecture too.

So yes it is possible to do lower precision compute with RDNA3 cores, but I would guess that except for the 7900XT and XTX, that even a 9060XT could beat in those low precision operations thanks to the new generation of cores. Allowing older generations (and RDNA2 doesn't even have matrix compute operations) to run new FSR would probably make things worse if the goal is to have more frames and people could be better served with an older FSR but at a better quality level.

comments.text:
@albert2006xp  Wrong on every point and completely sold on marketing fluff you've clearly never experienced first-hand. I have an RTX 5080 and never use ray tracing nor path tracing if the game won't run DLSS Quality at 90 FPS stable. These features are still in their infancy and won't run well for at least another 3-5 GPU generations. My "invented scenario" is CyberPunk 2077 with Path Tracing enabled.

DLSS Balanced and Performance looks dogshit. The artifacts from FG look even more dogshit. ~45 FPS before FG is not nearly enough as the input latency feels like dogshit and the overhead from enabling it drops the native framerate even lower. In your scenario it would drop it from ~45 to ~35, which feels like dogshit. Turning on FG at a higher FPS is detrimental not only to image quality but because, unless you have a 240-480Hz monitor, your FPS will run above the monitor refresh rate which causes screen tearing and poor frame pacing which, again, looks like dogshit. If you set a framerate cap 0.3ms below the refresh cycle of the monitor to prevent queued frames from tearing, you need to run the game natively at 34 FPS.

If you can't see how bad of an experience this is and then whine about enabling features that improve the visual fidelity by maybe 10% at the cost of 75% of your framerate and resolution, you're a massive goofball.

I'll gladly play with my 11ms stable latency rather than the 40ms latency I get with PT + FG, as I'm sure most would after the marketing honeymoon phase wears off.
